title: React Interview Prep — Day by Day
excerpt: A running, day-by-day set of React interview questions and answers — from JSX and components through state, props, and beyond — each with a full breakdown plus a tight, interview-ready answer to fall back on.

questions.question: What is React, and why is it used?

body.text: React is a JavaScript library (not a full framework) for building user interfaces, created by Facebook/Meta. Its core idea: build your UI as a tree of reusable components, and let React handle efficiently updating the DOM when your data changes.
Why it's used — the core problems it solves:

items: Manual DOM manipulation is slow and error-prone. Before React (and similar libraries), developers wrote imperative code like document.getElementById("x").innerHTML = ... all over the place, which becomes unmanageable as an app grows — you have to track exactly what changed and update it by hand.
React is declarative. You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React figures out how to update the actual DOM to match — you don't manually touch the DOM yourself.
Component-based architecture. UI is broken into small, reusable, independent pieces (buttons, forms, cards) that manage their own logic and can be composed together.
Virtual DOM (covered in depth later) — React keeps an in-memory representation of the UI and only updates the real DOM where necessary, rather than re-rendering everything.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: React is a declarative, component-based JavaScript library for building UIs. Instead of manually manipulating the DOM step by step, you describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React efficiently updates the real DOM to match — using a virtual DOM to minimize actual DOM operations. It's popular because it makes complex, interactive UIs easier to reason about and maintain through reusable, composable components.

questions.question: What are components in React?

body.text: A component is a self-contained, reusable piece of UI — it takes in data (via props) and returns what should be rendered (via JSX). Think of components as JavaScript functions that return UI instead of just a value.

items: Functional components — plain JavaScript functions (the modern standard, especially with Hooks).
Class components — ES6 classes extending React.Component (the older way).

body.text: Why components matter — composition:
Each piece is built, tested, and reasoned about independently, then assembled like building blocks. This is the fundamental unit of organization in every React app.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: A component is a reusable, self-contained building block of UI — essentially a function (or class) that accepts props as input and returns JSX describing what to render. Components let you break a complex UI into small, independent, composable pieces, which is the foundational organizing principle of any React application.

questions.question: What is JSX?

body.text: JSX (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup directly inside JavaScript. It's not valid JavaScript on its own — it gets compiled (typically by Babel) into regular React.createElement() calls before the browser ever sees it.
Key JSX rules interviewers test:

Why use it at all instead of plain createElement calls? JSX is purely a developer-experience improvement — it lets UI structure look like the HTML it produces, which is far more readable than deeply nested createElement calls. React works identically either way; JSX is optional but nearly universal in practice.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript, which Babel compiles into React.createElement() calls before it runs. It's not required to use React, but it makes component structure far more readable than the equivalent nested function calls. Key rules: it must return a single root element, uses {} to embed JS expressions, and uses className/camelCase attributes since it's ultimately still JavaScript, not HTML.

questions.question: How do you create a functional component in React?

body.text: The modern standard way to write React components — a plain JavaScript function that returns JSX.
With state (a preview of Hooks, covered in depth later):

Naming convention rule (worth knowing, it's not just style): component names must start with a capital letter (Welcome, not welcome) — this is how JSX distinguishes a custom component (<Welcome />) from a regular HTML tag (<welcome>, which React would treat as a literal, unknown HTML element).

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: A functional component is just a JavaScript function that returns JSX, optionally accepting props as its parameter. It's the modern standard way to write components, especially since Hooks let functional components hold state and side effects without needing a class. The one hard rule is the name must be capitalized, since that's how JSX tells a custom component apart from a plain HTML tag.

questions.question: How do you create a class component in React?

body.text: The older way to write components — an ES6 class extending React.Component, required to implement a render() method that returns JSX.
With state (the classic pre-Hooks pattern):

Why you rarely write these today: class components require this binding gymnastics (this.state, this.props, arrow functions or manual .bind() for event handlers), and lifecycle methods (componentDidMount, etc.) are more verbose than the equivalent Hooks. Since React 16.8 introduced Hooks, functional components can do everything class components can, with less boilerplate — so new code almost always uses functional components. You'll still see class components in older/legacy codebases, which is why interviewers still ask about them.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: A class component extends React.Component and must implement a render() method returning JSX. State lives on this.state, updated via this.setState(), and props are accessed via this.props. They were the only way to have state and lifecycle methods before Hooks arrived in React 16.8. I still need to recognize them for legacy code, but new components are functional, since Hooks provide the same capabilities with less boilerplate and no this binding issues.

questions.question: What is state in React?

body.text: State is data that's local to a component and can change over time — when it changes, React automatically re-renders that component (and its children) to reflect the new value.
Key properties of state:

items: Local and private to the component that owns it — a component can't directly read or set another component's state (only pass it down as props, or lift it up).
Changing state triggers a re-render — this is the whole mechanism that makes the UI "reactive" to data changes.

Should be treated as immutable — you never mutate state directly (state.count++ ❌), you always call the updater function (setCount(count + 1) ✅), because React relies on detecting a new value to know it needs to re-render.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: State is data a component owns internally that can change over time. When state updates via its setter function, React re-renders that component to reflect the new value. State is private to the component — you never mutate it directly, you always call the setter, since React relies on that call to know a re-render is needed.

questions.question: How does props work in React?

body.text: Props ("properties") are how a parent component passes data down to a child component — similar to function arguments, but for components.
Key properties of props:
Read-only from the child's perspective — a component receiving props can never modify them directly; only the parent that passed them can change what's sent down.

items: Flow one direction — parent → child only (this is called "unidirectional data flow" and is fundamental to how React apps are structured).
Can be anything — strings, numbers, objects, arrays, even functions (commonly used so a child can notify a parent of an event).

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: Props are how data flows from a parent component into a child, similar to function parameters. They're read-only — a child can never modify the props it receives, only the parent that owns the data can change what's passed down. This one-directional flow (parent to child) is core to how React apps stay predictable, and props can carry anything, including functions, which is how children typically communicate events back up to parents.

questions.question: What is the difference between state and props?

rows: internal data that changes over time

yes (when the parent's data changes, causing new props)

body.text: The mental model interviewers want to hear: state is a component's own private memory. Props are input a component receives from outside — think of props like function arguments, and state like a variable declared inside the function body. A component re-renders when either changes, but only state can be changed by that component itself; props can only ever be changed by whoever owns them (the parent).

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: State is data a component manages internally and can change itself via a setter — think of it as private memory. Props are data passed in from a parent, and are read-only from the receiving component's perspective — think of them like function arguments. Both trigger re-renders when they change, but a component only controls its own state; it never controls the props it receives, since those belong to whoever passed them down.

questions.question: How do you pass data between components?

body.text: There are four directions data can move between components in React, each with its own mechanism. Here's the full picture at a glance before working through each one:

body.code:
Parent -> Child (props)              Child -> Parent (callback)
+----------+   name="Hi"    +---------+   onSend("Hi!")   back up
|  Parent  | -------------> |  Child  | ------------------> to Parent
+----------+                +---------+   (calls the fn it was given)

Sibling <-> Sibling                    Distant / deeply nested
                                        +---------------------------+
+-----------+   +-----------+           | <ThemeContext.Provider>   |
| Sibling A |   | Sibling B |           |     ...                   |
+-----+-----+   +-----^-----+           |       ...                 |
      |  state lives in the             |         DeeplyNested      |
      +--> shared PARENT ---------------->  reads it directly,      |
           ("lifting state up")         |  no props threaded down   |
                                        +---------------------------+

body.text: Parent → Child (props — the simplest, most common case):
Child → Parent (via a callback function passed as a prop):
There's no built-in way for a child to directly modify a parent's state — the parent has to explicitly hand down a function the child can call, which then updates the parent's own state.
Sibling ↔ Sibling (no direct path — must go through a shared parent, aka “lifting state up”):
Distant/deeply nested components (Context API):

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: Data flows down via props from parent to child. To send data back up, the parent passes a callback function as a prop, which the child calls to communicate an event or value. There's no direct sibling-to-sibling communication — it has to go through a shared parent, which is the basis of 'lifting state up.' For data needed across many nested levels without manually threading it through every component, Context API avoids the prop-drilling problem.

questions.question: What is the purpose of render() in React?

body.text: render() is a required method on class components that returns the JSX describing what the UI should look like for the current state/props. It's the class-component equivalent of what a functional component's function body does — every time state or props change, React calls render() again to figure out the updated UI.
Key rules about render():

items: Must be pure — given the same this.props and this.state, it should always return the same JSX. It should not modify state (calling setState inside render() causes an infinite loop), interact with the DOM directly, or trigger side effects like API calls.
Called automatically by React whenever state or props change — you never call it manually.
Can return null to render nothing.

body.text: The functional component equivalent: functional components don't have a render() method — the function body itself is the render logic; whatever JSX you return from the function serves the exact same purpose.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: render() is the required method on a class component that returns the JSX for the current state and props — React calls it automatically whenever either changes, to determine what the UI should look like. It must be a pure function with no side effects or state mutations inside it. In functional components, there's no separate render() method — the function body itself plays that role, since whatever JSX it returns is what gets rendered.

questions.question: How do you use conditional rendering in React?

body.text: Since JSX is just JavaScript, you can use normal JS control flow to decide what to render.
The gotcha interviewers love with &&: if the left-hand value is 0 (a “falsy” number, not false), React will actually render the literal 0 on screen instead of nothing:

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: Since JSX is just JavaScript, conditional rendering uses normal JS constructs — if/else before the return for branching logic, ternaries inline within JSX for simple either/or cases, and && for an all-or-nothing render. The classic gotcha with && is that a falsy-but-non-boolean left side, like 0, gets rendered literally instead of being treated as 'nothing' — so I make sure the left side of && is an actual boolean.

questions.question: What are keys in React lists, and why are they important?

body.text: When rendering a list of elements, React needs a stable, unique identifier per item to efficiently figure out which items changed, were added, or were removed between renders — that's what the key prop is for.

Why this matters — how React's reconciliation actually uses keys: React compares the previous render's list against the new one using keys to match up which DOM elements correspond to which data items. Without a stable key, React can't tell “this is the same item, just moved” from “this is a brand new item” — leading it to unnecessarily re-render, lose internal component state (like a text input's typed value), or even show the wrong item's state at a given position.

body.code:
Before render          After reorder (B moved to front)
key=A  Priya           key=B  Rahul      <- React matches by KEY,
key=B  Rahul           key=A  Priya         not by position
key=C  Amit            key=C  Amit

With stable keys:   React sees "A, B, C just moved" -> reuses the
                    same DOM nodes & component state, just reorders them.

With index as key:  position 0 was "A", is now "B" -> React thinks
                    the ITEM at position 0 changed -> may re-render it
                    and drag along any local state (e.g. a typed input)
                    from the wrong row.

body.text: The classic mistake — using array index as key:

This seems to work fine for static lists, but breaks if the list can be reordered, filtered, or items inserted/removed from the middle — because the index no longer reliably identifies “the same item” across renders, causing React to misattribute state to the wrong item (e.g., an input's typed text jumping to the wrong row after a reorder).

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: Keys give React a stable identity for each item in a list, so it can correctly match items between renders during reconciliation — figuring out what was added, removed, or reordered, rather than re-rendering everything or losing component state. I always use a stable unique ID from the data itself, never the array index, since index-based keys break when the list can be reordered or filtered — React can end up attaching the wrong internal state to the wrong visual position.

questions.question: How do you handle events in React?

body.text: React events look like DOM events, but with important differences: camelCase naming, and you pass a function reference, not a string.
The classic beginner mistake — calling the function instead of passing it:

body.code:
<button onClick={handleClick()}>Click</button>   // ❌ runs immediately on render, not on click!
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click</button>      // ✅ passes the function reference
<button onClick={() => handleClick()}>Click</button>  // ✅ also correct — wrapped, runs on click

body.text: SyntheticEvent — React wraps native browser events in its own cross-browser wrapper object (SyntheticEvent) that normalizes behavior across different browsers, so you don't need browser-specific event-handling code. It has the same interface as native events (.preventDefault(), .target, .stopPropagation(), etc.).

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: React events use camelCase naming and you pass a function reference rather than a string, unlike inline HTML onclick. React wraps native events in a SyntheticEvent object that normalizes behavior across browsers while exposing the same familiar API — preventDefault, target, and so on. The most common mistake is writing onClick={handleClick()}, which calls the function immediately during render instead of passing it to be called later, on the actual click.

questions.question: What is setState() in React?

body.text: The method used in class components to update state and trigger a re-render. (In functional components, this role is played by the setter function returned from useState — e.g., setCount — which behaves similarly but isn't literally called setState.)
Two critical behaviors interviewers test:
1. setState() is asynchronous/batched — React doesn't update state immediately; it batches multiple setState calls together for performance, then applies them and re-renders once.

2. It merges, doesn't replace, the state object — calling setState({ count: 5 }) only updates count, leaving other state keys untouched (this is different from useState's setter, which fully replaces the value unless you spread manually).
The safe pattern for updates that depend on the previous state — pass a function instead of an object, since it always receives the actual latest state, avoiding stale-value bugs from batching:

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: setState() updates a class component's state and schedules a re-render. It's asynchronous and batched for performance, so reading this.state immediately after calling it can show a stale value. It also merges the update into existing state rather than replacing the whole object. For updates that depend on the previous state, I use the functional form — setState(prevState => ...) — to avoid bugs from stale values when multiple updates are batched together.

questions.question: What is a pure component?

body.text: A component that only re-renders when its props or state actually change — determined via a shallow comparison — instead of re-rendering every time its parent re-renders regardless of whether anything relevant changed.
The functional-component equivalent is React.memo() (covered fully on Day 9):
The critical caveat — “shallow” comparison:
This is why passing inline object/array/function literals as props to a PureComponent/React.memo component often silently defeats the whole optimization — each render creates a brand-new reference.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: A PureComponent automatically implements shouldComponentUpdate with a shallow prop/state comparison, skipping re-renders when nothing relevant actually changed — an optimization over a regular component, which re-renders on every parent re-render by default. The catch is that the comparison is shallow: it compares object/array props by reference, not deep equality, so passing a new object literal as a prop every render defeats the optimization even if the content is identical.

questions.question: What is the virtual DOM?

body.text: A lightweight in-memory JavaScript representation of the actual DOM. React uses it to figure out the minimal set of real DOM changes needed, instead of re-rendering the entire page on every update.
The process, step by step:

items: When state/props change, React builds a new virtual DOM tree representing the updated UI.
React compares (“diffs”) this new tree against the previous virtual DOM tree — this process is called reconciliation.
React calculates the minimal set of actual differences.
React applies only those specific changes to the real DOM — not a full re-render of everything.

body.text: Why this matters — the actual DOM is expensive to manipulate: every real DOM update can trigger reflow/repaint, which is comparatively slow. Diffing in-memory JavaScript objects (the virtual DOM) is much cheaper, so React minimizes the number of expensive real-DOM touches by batching and calculating the smallest possible update first.

body.code:
state/props change
         |
         v
  build NEW virtual DOM tree
         |
         v
  DIFF vs previous virtual DOM tree   <-- "reconciliation"
         |
         v
  compute minimal patch list
  (e.g. "only this text node changed")
         |
         v
  apply ONLY those patches to the real DOM
  (no full page re-render)

body.text: A common misconception worth correcting in an interview: the virtual DOM isn't inherently “faster than the DOM” in some magical universal sense — it's that React's diffing + batching strategy generally results in fewer, more targeted real DOM operations than naive manual re-rendering would, especially as UI complexity grows. For very simple, small updates, hand-written vanilla JS DOM manipulation could technically be faster — the virtual DOM's win is in developer ergonomics (write declarative code) combined with reasonably efficient updates at scale, not raw benchmark speed for every single case.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: The virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the UI that React uses to compute the minimal set of real DOM changes needed after a state or props update. When something changes, React builds a new virtual tree, diffs it against the previous one — a process called reconciliation — and applies only the actual differences to the real DOM, rather than re-rendering everything. This matters because real DOM operations are comparatively expensive, so minimizing and batching them keeps updates fast even as the UI grows in complexity.

questions.question: Explain the concept of lifting state up.

body.text: When two or more sibling components need to share and stay in sync with the same data, you move ("lift") that state to their closest common parent, which then passes it down to both as props.

body.code:
BEFORE — each child has its own private box, they can't see each other

   Parent
   |
   +-- NameInput   [ own state: "" ]   <-- these two don't know
   +-- Greeting    [ own state: "" ]   <-- about each other at all

AFTER — state moves UP to the parent, both children read from the SAME source

   Parent  [ state: name = "" ]   <-- single source of truth
     |         |
     v         v
   NameInput   Greeting
   (props)     (props)

   Now Greeting always shows the CURRENT text typed into NameInput.

body.text: Easy beginner example: imagine a text box where you type your name, and right next to it a sentence that says "Hello, <name>!" and updates live as you type. If the input box kept the typed name in its own private state, the Greeting sibling would have no way to know what was typed — it can't reach into another component's state. So instead, the name is stored in the parent, and both the input and the greeting just read from that same shared value.

Now Greeting always shows exactly what's typed into NameInput, because both read from the same name value stored in their shared parent — impossible when each managed its own separate, disconnected state.

One more example, this time a common real-world pattern — an e-commerce cart badge. The "Add to Cart" buttons live inside a ProductList component, but the cart count badge is shown in a completely separate Navbar component — two siblings that both need access to the same number. Clicking a button in ProductList has to somehow update the badge inside Navbar, and the only way to do that is to lift the cartCount state up to their common parent.

Same pattern as the name/greeting example: neither ProductList nor Navbar owns the cart count itself — they only receive it (or a way to change it) as props from their shared parent, which stays the single source of truth. That's why clicking "Add to Cart" in one sibling instantly updates the badge in a totally different sibling.

Why this matters — the underlying principle: React data flows one direction (parent → child, from Day 3). Since siblings can't talk to each other directly, the only way to share state between them is to move that state up to a level both can access, then pass it back down as props.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: Lifting state up means moving shared state from individual sibling components to their closest common parent, which then passes the data (and update functions) back down as props. It's the standard React pattern for keeping multiple components in sync, since siblings have no direct communication path — the only shared point of truth they both have access to is a common ancestor.

questions.question: What is prop drilling in React?

body.text: The problem that occurs when you have to pass props down through many intermediate components that don't actually need that data themselves — they're just relaying it further down to a deeply nested child that does.

body.code:
App [ has: user ] | | passes user down just to forward it... v Layout [ user -> just relays it, never reads it ] | v Sidebar [ user -> just relays it, never reads it ] | v UserProfile [ user -> FINALLY used here:

{user.name}

] Layout and Sidebar are just "pass-through" pipes carrying data they never actually use — that's prop drilling.

body.text: Layout and Sidebar have no use for user themselves — they're just forced to accept and pass it along because it's the only path down to UserProfile. As an app grows, this becomes tedious to maintain and makes components harder to reuse (they're now coupled to props they don't even use).
The fix — Context API (you'll cover this fully on Day 7), which lets deeply nested components read shared data directly without every intermediate level having to know about or forward it:

Other alternatives worth mentioning: component composition (passing components as children instead of drilling data), or state management libraries like Redux (you'll cover Redux in the Advanced section) for larger, more complex apps.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: Prop drilling happens when data has to pass through several intermediate components that don't need it themselves, just to reach a deeply nested child that does — making those middle components unnecessarily coupled to data they never use. The standard fix for moderate cases is the Context API, which lets a deeply nested component read shared data directly without every level in between having to forward it. For larger apps, a dedicated state management library is often used instead.

questions.question: How can you optimize a React application?

body.text: A broad topic — interviewers want to see you know several levers, not just one deep answer.
Preventing unnecessary re-renders:
Code-level techniques:

items: Code splitting / lazy loading (React.lazy + Suspense, covered Day 8 & 21) — load parts of the app only when needed, reducing initial bundle size.
Virtualization for long lists — libraries like react-window render only the visible portion of a huge list instead of all items at once.
Keys done right (Day 3) — stable, correct keys avoid unnecessary re-renders/re-mounts in lists.
Avoid inline object/array/function literals as props when passing to memoized components (Day 4's PureComponent gotcha) — they create new references every render, defeating memoization.
Debounce/throttle expensive handlers (search inputs, scroll listeners — recall from your JS plan, Day 9).

body.text: Bundle/loading-level techniques:

items: Minimize bundle size — tree-shaking, removing unused dependencies.
Image optimization — lazy-load images, use appropriately sized/compressed formats.
Server-side rendering / static generation (Day 17, 21) — faster initial paint for users.

body.text: Easy beginner way to picture it: imagine a big Excel sheet with 10,000 rows. If you re-draw all 10,000 rows every time one cell changes, the app feels slow. Optimization is just a set of tricks to redraw only what actually changed (React.memo, useMemo), load only what's currently needed (code splitting, virtualization), and avoid tricking React into thinking something changed when it didn't (avoiding new object/array literals as props).

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: Optimization happens at several levels: preventing unnecessary re-renders with React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback; reducing initial load with code splitting and lazy loading; using list virtualization for long lists instead of rendering everything; and being careful not to pass new object/function references as props to memoized components, which silently defeats the optimization. In practice, I'd profile with React DevTools' Profiler first to find the actual bottleneck rather than optimizing blindly.

questions.question: What are React fragments?

body.text: A way to group multiple elements without adding an extra wrapper DOM node. Recall from Day 3 that JSX requires a single root element — Fragments satisfy that rule without polluting the actual rendered HTML with a meaningless extra <div>.

body.code:
Wrapping in a
Wrapping in a Fragment (extra node in real DOM) (NO extra node in real DOM)
      <- invalid!
    • Item 1
      • <- direct child, valid
    • Item 1
    • Item 2
      • <- direct child, valid
    • Item 2
A
    expects
  • to be its DIRECT child. A Fragment groups elements in JSX without showing up as a node in the real DOM at all.

body.text: Easy beginner example: think of a Fragment like an invisible plastic bag you use to carry two items together in code — but when you actually place the items on the shelf (the real DOM), the bag disappears and only the two items remain, sitting directly on the shelf. A <div> wrapper, by contrast, is like leaving the bag on the shelf too — an extra thing nobody asked for.
Why avoiding extra <div>s actually matters:

items: Invalid HTML in some contexts — e.g., a <div> isn't a valid direct child of <table>, <ul>, or <select>, so an unnecessary wrapper can literally break rendering/semantics in those cases.
CSS layout issues — extra wrapper divs can interfere with Flexbox/Grid layouts that expect direct children to be the actual content elements.
Cleaner, smaller DOM tree — fewer unnecessary nodes overall.

body.text: One case where you need the full <React.Fragment key={...}> syntax instead of <>: when rendering a list of Fragments, since the shorthand <> doesn't support the key prop:

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: A Fragment lets you group multiple JSX elements and satisfy React's single-root-element rule without adding an actual extra node to the rendered DOM. The shorthand <>...</> is the common syntax, but I use the full <React.Fragment key={...}> form when rendering a list of fragments, since the shorthand doesn't support keys. It matters because unnecessary wrapper divs can break valid HTML nesting rules — like inside a <table> or <ul> — and can interfere with CSS layouts that expect direct children.
